name: Boost.Bloom (block / multiblock filter configurations)
workload: Insertion and successful/unsuccessful/mixed lookup of int keys (N=1M) comparing boost::bloom::filter's classical single-array configuration (filter<int,K>) against its block/multiblock/fast_multiblock32 configurations at equal bits-per-item budgets.
claimed_speedup: ~2-4x faster insertion and lookup for block/multiblock variants vs the library's own classical Bloom filter at matched c (bits/item): e.g. at c=8, insertion 3.99-5.07ns (block/multiblock) vs 11.04ns (classical); lookup 4.60-5.12ns vs 12.08-18.15ns; at c=16, insertion 5.02-5.55ns vs 20.28ns; lookup 5.62-6.02ns vs 18.12-21.45ns (GCC 14, x64)
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14, x64, -march=native (release settings); other columns for Clang 15/18, VS2022, x86 also given
stars_or_usage: 37 stars; official Boost library since Boost 1.89, distributed via vcpkg (boost-bloom) and Conan
tradeoffs: Header-only, C++11. Block/multiblock variants trade a small FPR increase (at matched c) for large speed gains by confining all K bit-sets to one or few cache lines; classical filter<int,K> remains available for lowest FPR at a given c.
caveats: Benchmark repo (boostorg/boost_bloom_benchmarks) states compiler and flags but never names the actual CPU model used (CI runners), so it falls short of Tier A despite public, runnable benchmark code. Numbers are the project's own, not independently reproduced.
found_via: vcpkg port listing (`boost-bloom`, confirmed via `gh api repos/microsoft/vcpkg/contents/ports`), cross-checked against boostorg/bloom repo

name: fastbloom
workload: Membership insert/query throughput compared against other Rust Bloom filter crates (bloom, bloomfilter, probabilistic-collections, sbbf-rs) using each crate's default/best hasher, per the linked bench-bloom-filters harness.
claimed_speedup: "2-20 times faster ... than existing Bloom filter implementations" with equal or better false-positive accuracy (exact per-crate charts hosted as images in the bench-bloom-filters repo, not reproduced as text on this page)
hardware: AMD Ryzen 9 5900X 12-Core Processor (3.70 GHz), 64-bit OS, x64
tradeoffs: Rust-only, no C API; speed comes from deriving many index bits from a single real hash (hash composition) instead of K independent hashes. Has an AtomicBloomFilter for lock-free concurrent use.
caveats: Benchmark chart is the project's own (bench-bloom-filters repo, no stated license), rustc version/flags not given on the page, and results are shown as images rather than a numeric table, so exact per-crate ns/op figures could not be quoted verbatim.
found_via: crates.io API query "bloom filter" sorted by downloads (crate: fastbloom)

name: rbloom
workload: Insert 10,000,000 float keys into a Bloom(10_000_000, 0.01) filter, then look up all 10,000,000 keys, compared against other Python Bloom filter packages (pybloomfiltermmap3, pybloom3, Flor, bloom-filter2).
claimed_speedup: 2.52s (rbloom) vs 4.78s (pybloomfiltermmap3), 46.76s (pybloom3), 76.94s (Flor), 165.54s (bloom-filter2) -- up to ~65x faster than the slowest compared library (derived from page data)
hardware: Apple M1 Pro ("confirmed to be proportional to runtimes on an Intel machine")
tradeoffs: Implemented in Rust with a Python API (PyO3), compiled against a stable ABI (abi3) for portability at a small perf cost vs building from source; does not use mmap so no zero-copy persistence like pybloomfiltermmap3.
caveats: Benchmark script (benchmarks/compare.py) is in-repo but rustc/maturin flags used to build the wheel for the timing run are not stated on the page; comparison is against other Python bindings, not a bare-metal C/C++ Bloom filter.

name: Register-Blocked SIMD Bit-Pattern Bloom Filter (bloomfilter_benchmarks)
workload: Per-operation cycle count for insert/lookup on Basic, Blocked, Register-Blocked, and Bit-Pattern Bloom filter variants (scalar and AVX2) across small-to-large filter sizes.
claimed_speedup: 22x increase in throughput over the classic ("Basic") Bloom filter: Basic ~56-254 cycles/op, Blocked ~30 cycles/op, Register-Blocked ~20 cycles/op scalar / ~5 cycles/op AVX2, Bit-Pattern ~2.5 cycles/op with AVX2 SIMD
tradeoffs: Header-only (bloom_filters.h); Bit-Pattern/register-blocked variants need AVX2 and trade a small FPR/space overhead for cache-locality and vectorized bit tests. Blog author is independent (Sasha Krassovsky), not affiliated with a Bloom filter vendor.
caveats: No repo-level LICENSE badge on the blog post itself, but the linked GitHub repo carries an MIT LICENSE file. Benchmark uses nanobench (in-repo) and raw CSV outputs are checked in for reproducibility.
found_via: HN Algolia search "bloom filter faster" tags=story -> "Modern Bloom Filters: 22x Faster" (save-buffer.github.io/bloom_filter.html, redirects to blog.krassovsky.com)

name: Clubcard
workload: Encoding Mozilla's CRLite certificate-revocation-status dataset (816 million certificates, 795 issuers, 11.7 million revoked) as a set-membership filter, replacing the existing Bloom filter cascade used in production.
claimed_speedup: 8.5 MB (Clubcard, Ribbon-filter based) vs 19.3 MB (existing Bloom filter cascade, published 2024-08-29) -- a 56% size reduction (derived from page data: 1 - 8.5/19.3 ~= 0.56)
stars_or_usage: 24 stars; used in Mozilla's production CRLite pipeline for Firefox
tradeoffs: Exact (no false positives for encoded set) membership filter built on Ribbon filters plus a two-level cascade; construction is offline/batch (not designed for online inserts like a classic Bloom filter). API and serialization format explicitly marked unstable ("work in progress").
caveats: This is a memory/size comparison from one production snapshot, not a timing benchmark; no CPU/compiler details apply. The 56% figure is against Mozilla's own prior Bloom-cascade encoding of the same dataset, not a generic third-party Bloom filter.
found_via: crates.io API query "xor filter" sorted by downloads, surfaced "clubcard" crate (repository mozilla/clubcard)

name: Dynamic Cuckoo Filter (DCF)
workload: Insert/query/delete/compact 1,000,000 items at expected FPR 0.0005, comparing DCF (cuckoo-hashing based, linked homogeneous cuckoo-filter blocks) against a Dynamic Bloom Filter of matched actual FPR.
claimed_speedup: Space: 2.5MB (DCF) vs 10.9MB (DBF), ~4x smaller. Time: insert 1.08s vs 1.69s (1.5x), query 1.05s vs 1.92s (1.8x), delete 1.36s vs 3.35s (2.4x) for 1M items (numbers and ratio labels both given verbatim in the README results table)
tradeoffs: Adds reliable item deletion plus dynamic capacity extension/reduction on top of standard Cuckoo Filters; requires OpenSSL for hashing and a compact/rehash operation to reclaim space from removed building blocks.
caveats: Baseline is Dynamic Bloom Filter, a variant, not the plain incumbent Bloom filter, so recorded with baseline_in_list=false. Compiler and flags are not stated (just `make`), and hardware is an old, low-end laptop CPU from 2011-era, so absolute numbers may not generalize to modern hardware; repo unmaintained since 2017.
found_via: gh search repos "cuckoo filter" language:C++ --sort stars

name: Better Choice Cuckoo Filter (BCF)
workload: Insert 1,048,576 items (12-bit fingerprints) using power-of-two-choices bucket selection, comparing average relocation count and insertion latency against the standard Cuckoo Filter (efficient/cuckoofilter design).
claimed_speedup: 35% fewer average relocations and 25% lower item-insertion latency vs standard Cuckoo Filter
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2670 0 @ 2.60GHz, Red Hat Enterprise Linux Server 6.2
tradeoffs: Only changes the insertion-time bucket-selection rule (pick the less-loaded of the two candidate buckets); lookup/delete paths are unchanged from a standard Cuckoo Filter, so read performance is unaffected while write performance and load factor improve.
caveats: Backed by a peer-reviewed paper (Wang, Chen, Liao, Zhang, Jin, "The Power of Better Choice: Reducing Relocations in Cuckoo Filter", ICDCS 2019) which is why this is rated Tier B despite the repo itself lacking stated compiler/flags. Repository ships with no LICENSE file (GitHub reports license as "Other"/NOASSERTION), so treat code as reference-only, not redistributable.
found_via: gh search repos "cuckoo filter" language:C++ --sort stars

name: Entry-Extensible Cuckoo Filter (E2CF)
workload: Membership query and insertion over items with configurable false-positive rate, using adjacent-bucket entry extension to avoid discrete memory accesses, compared to existing (unnamed-in-README) cuckoo filter designs.
claimed_speedup: Reduces query time by up to 82% and insertion time by up to 28% vs existing cuckoo filter designs
hardware: Intel CPU @ 2.60GHz, 64GB RAM, 64-byte cache line, Red Hat Enterprise Linux Server 6.2
tradeoffs: Uses adjacent, sequentially-addressed buckets plus asynchronous extension and fine-grained splitting to reduce cache misses on query; from the same research group as DCF and BCF, so likely compares against the standard Cuckoo Filter, but the README does not name the baseline explicitly.
caveats: README says "compared to existing designs" without naming the exact baseline implementation or citing a specific paper/DOI, and gives no CPU model number (just "Intel 2.60GHz") or compiler/flags -- weaker methodology disclosure than the group's DCF/BCF repos, and confidence is lowered accordingly.
found_via: gh search repos "cuckoo filter" language:C++ --sort stars
